column1: # TRANSFORMATION: emit(select, table) (G9 phase 6,
# docs/design/EMIT.0.md). Apply-templates: for every node of `select`,
# in order, the first template whose `match` the node unifies with is
# taken and its `body` instantiated AGAINST THAT NODE.
# Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect
# THE RESULT IS FLAT, and that is a constraint rather than a
# convenience: a body element that is itself a list SPLICES, which is
# what makes a nested dispatch compose into one sequence rather than a
# tree of them.
# Every expectation below was obtained by running BOTH engines and
# diffing, error text included.
# DISPATCH. First match wins, in TABLE ORDER, by unifiability -- the
# same question `match` and `filter` ask, answered the same way. A
# table of one may be written as the template map itself, told apart
# by kind.
emit-dispatch
emit-first-match-wins
emit-table-one-map
emit-body-order
# ORDER IS FIXED the way canon already fixes it: source order for a
# list, sorted-key order for a map.
emit-map-selection
# AN EMPTY SELECTION EMITS NOTHING, and that is the whole conditional
# mechanism -- it is why no `when` directive exists. A dispatch over a
# filter that selects nothing is the conditional written as data.
emit-empty-selection
emit-empty-map-selection
emit-of-filter
emit-of-filter-none
# SPLICING, and the nesting it makes possible.
emit-splice
emit-nested-inline
# A NESTED TABLE IS THE INNER emit's, and its SELECTOR is the channel:
# argument 0 is bound at the outer node, everything past it is the
# inner dispatch's to bind. A nested selector that is ABSOLUTE binds
# nothing at all, and the outer node reaches the inner rules through
# what the selector selects, exactly as it does when the selector is
# relative.
emit-nested-absolute-selection
# THE TWO BINDINGS. `_` is the matched node; a RELATIVE reference is a
# field of it. The binding is emit's, not path resolution's: a
# relative path is a count taken wherever a value comes to rest, and
# the nodes of a computed selection come to rest nowhere. An ABSOLUTE
# reference is untouched and still reads the document root.
emit-place
emit-relative-ref
emit-relative-ref-deep
emit-absolute-ref
# A NAMED TABLE IS A PLACEHELD `emit`. A table written at a document
# position is DRIVEN there -- a body's relative references resolve
# against wherever it sits and miss -- so the position that holds one
# unevaluated is the one position the language never drives: a call's
# template argument. `emit(_, T)` is that position with the selection
# left open, and it reads as what it is, an apply-templates waiting
# for its nodes. Passing them by call and by meet are the same
# dispatch. This is also XSLT's MODE, with no keyword: a mode is a
# table used from several sites, and naming a value is something the
# language already does.
emit-named-table-two-sites
emit-meet-form
# AND THIS IS WHY THE DISPATCH IS A BUILTIN. A rule set that names
# itself walks a nested tree into nested output -- the first example
# in every XSLT tutorial, and not expressible at any length as an
# inlined expansion, because a template that reaches itself has no
# finite one. Termination is the SELECTION's: each dispatch descends
# into a finite bag that already exists, and a selection that empties
# emits nothing.
emit-recursive
# THE SHAPE CODES, all class `parse`: what is wrong is the CALL as the
# author wrote it. A rule needs both halves -- one with no pattern
# would claim every node by accident, one with no body would claim a
# node and emit nothing -- and a body is a list even when it holds one
# piece, which is what lets bodies splice.
emit-data-integer
emit-data-string
emit-table-scalar
emit-template-not-map
emit-template-no-match
emit-template-in-list-no-match
emit-template-no-body
emit-body-not-list
# NO MATCH IS AN ERROR, not an empty answer, and the report names the
# patterns that were tried -- the admissible-alternatives shape.
# XSLT's built-in rule copies an unhandled node's string value into
# the result, which for code output means model data landing silently
# in the middle of a source file; it is the single worst default in
# the prior art and it is refused. A template whose `match` is `any`,
# written last, is how a document says it meant to allow the rest.
emit-none
emit-none-tried
# A REFERENCE THE NODE CANNOT ANSWER is reported against the NODE,
# where the author can see what was tried, rather than missing
# somewhere else as no_path. Only a chain of plain names is a field: a
# parent step has no answer at a node that is an origin rather than a
# position.
emit-ref-missing
emit-ref-parent-step
# UNFIRED, a dispatch canons as its CALL, which reparses to the same
# value -- so canon convergence holds for a model that has not
# finished. Reaching that state takes a selection that never settles
# (`1+true` is the stuck operation budget.tsv uses), because a
# dispatch whose selection settles fires.
emit-unfired-canon
emit-literal-canon
# A VARIABLE PATH SEGMENT is not a name until something resolves it, and
# the binding happens before that: `$bar` is bound to "hello" for the
# shared rows, and the field it would name is refused at the node rather
# than left to resolve somewhere else.
emit-ref-var-segment
# A BODY ELEMENT IS AN ORDINARY VALUE, and the node binding reaches
# through whatever it is written as -- a map, a nested list, a
# preference, a conjunct, a disjunct. A disjunct that stays open is
# refused at generation exactly as one written anywhere else is; the
# binding does not make it concrete.
emit-body-map
emit-body-list-ref
emit-body-pref
emit-body-conjunct
emit-body-disjunct
# A NODE NEED NOT BE A RECORD. Anything with a pattern that admits it
# dispatches; a scalar node simply has no field for a reference to name.
emit-scalar-nodes
emit-ref-scalar-node
emit-ref-list-index
emit-ref-list-index-past-end
emit-ref-through-scalar
# A CALL IS NOT A TABLE. `emit`'s table argument is never driven, so a
# generator written there arrives as the call it is, and a call is
# neither a list of rules nor one rule.
emit-table-call
